If overvoltage or short circuit conditions occur in the DC power supply system, the regulator and overload protection device disconnects the generator from the DC bus; this fail condition can be reset by ground crew only. If both generators fail, the voice information and warning system gives a corresponding message as well.

08
Section 1 · pages 1-50 to 1-51

Hydraulic power

Two independent systems: the main hydraulic system and the hydraulic boost system (Figure FO-11). Both are powered by variable volume piston pumps, one for each system, flanged to and driven by the GBX, operating at a pressure between 190 kp/cm² (19 MPa) and 220 kp/cm² (22 MPa).

Main system provides

  • Operation of the second chamber of the hydraulic actuators of the tailerons, the ailerons, the rudders, and of the hydraulic actuator of the AOA limiter system (COC).
  • Extension and retraction of landing gear, flaps/LEF and speedbrakes.
  • Control of the variable air intake ramps, the actuator of the APU exhaust door, the nose wheel steering and damper system and the hydraulic actuator of the rudder feel force system.

Boost system provides

  • Operation of the first chamber of the dual chamber hydraulic actuators of the tailerons, the ailerons, the rudder and the hydraulic actuator of the AOA limiter system (COC).

Reservoirs, accumulators, cooling

Both hydraulic fluid reservoirs are located inside fuel tank 3 and ensure normal operation of the pumps under all flight conditions; due to the two-chamber configuration they feed the pumps even during negative g flight. They are filled up as a closed system through filler caps in the return lines, and are pressurized with low-pressure compressed air from the main pneumatic system through a pressure regulator valve to avoid cavitation at the pump inlets. Safety relief valves prevent overpressurization.

Accumulators in the main and boost systems store a supply of high pressure fluid to damp pressure surges caused by sudden variations in flow demands. Both accumulators are charged with nitrogen at 80 kp/cm² (8 MPa), which corresponds with the marking PAK on the combined pressure indicator. Installing the reservoirs in fuel tank 3 gives adequate cooling of the hydraulic fluid by heat exchange with fuel.

Protection and emergency pump

A pressure limiter and isolation valve is installed in the high-pressure lines of the main system: if the pressure drops below 130 kp/cm² (13 MPa) it disconnects all systems except the flight controls and supplies only one chamber of tailerons, ailerons, rudders, flaps/LEF and AOA limiter actuator. Pressure relief valves in the main and the boost system open at 240 kp/cm² (24 MPa) and discharge fluid into the return lines.

An emergency hydraulic pump installed in the hydraulic boost system supports basic control functions at an RPM of both engines of at least 85 %. Although the pump delivers pressure up to 240 kp/cm² (24 MPa), the delivery rate permits only severely degraded aircraft control. It is driven by fuel pressure and is activated automatically whenever the system pressure of both systems drops below 100 kp/cm² (10 MPa); it can also be activated manually with the EMERGENCY HYDR PUMP switch on the control panel next to the CHUTE JETTISON button.

Controls and indications

Both reservoirs have level transmitters connected to level indicators installed in the central refuelling control panel in the left main wheel well. The actual pressures of the main system and of the boost system are displayed on the combined pressure indicator (CPI), which uses 115 VAC from the AC generator.

The CPI transmitters are connected to the nitrogen gas side of the accumulators, so the CPI indicates nitrogen pressure PAK when hydraulic system pressure is zero. Whenever one engine has reached a minimum of 20 % RPM, the hydraulic pressures must be within the green areas. The green areas contain two markers, QO (system pressure with none of the actuators moving, i.e. zero delivery) and QM (system pressure with the hydraulic actuators moving with maximum velocity).

During engine start at low ambient temperatures and increased hydraulic fluid flow rate, the hydraulic pressure indication may drop into the yellow area.

Whenever the pressure of one of the hydraulic systems drops below 100 kp/cm² (10 MPa), the respective warning indications are displayed; if pressure is regained, they extinguish. The AFCS is disengaged if the pressure in both systems drops below 100 kp/cm² (10 MPa) until pressure is regained.

Warning

With the emergency hydraulic pump running, boost hydraulic system pressure may be regained at low or zero delivery rates. Therefore, extinguishing of the double hydraulic system indications must be considered temporary and the situation continued to be treated as a double hydraulic system failure.

IndicationFault / effectVIWAS (German)

09
Section 1 · pages 1-52 to 1-53

Pneumatic power

Two independent systems — main and emergency (Figure 1-24). Several pressure bottles are charged to 150 kp/cm² (15 MPa) gaseous nitrogen; to ensure drag chute operation an additional pressure bottle charged to 63 kp/cm² (6.3 MPa) is located close to the drag chute compartment.

Main system12.4 l
Emergency system10 l
Radar ventilation2 l
Storage pressure150 kp/cm² (15 MPa)

Main system operates

  • Wheel brakes
  • Canopy and canopy seals
  • Drag chute
  • Fuel shut-off valves
  • Radio and radar equipment pressurization
  • Venting of the hydraulic reservoirs
  • GT: periscope system

Emergency system operates

  • Emergency gear extension
  • Emergency braking of the main wheels

A common charging valve and a pressure indicator are located in the left main landing gear bay; crossfeed between the systems is prevented by check valves in the interconnecting lines. Two scales on the CPI (right side of the main vertical cockpit console) display main and emergency pneumatic system pressure; for normal operation the pressure must remain in the green area.

Note

The pneumatic power supply system is not charged during flight.

10
Section 1 · pages 1-54 to 1-58

Landing gear and brakes

Retractable tricycle landing gear, electrically controlled and hydraulically actuated by the main hydraulic system. DC power from the generator or the batteries is required for operation. Retraction time 9 to 10 sec, extension time 7 to 8 sec; simultaneously the APU doors are opened or closed respectively.

Main landing gear

Each main gear is hydraulically retracted and extended. In the extended position the gear is locked down by an internal mechanical lock in each gear actuating cylinder. With the handle in RETRACTED the gear will retract; as it retracts, the wheels are automatically braked to a stop. When the gear is up and locked, brake pressure is automatically released. The main gear retracts forward and is enclosed by three fairing doors; it is mechanically locked in the wheel wells.

The right main gear strut is equipped with a shock detector plate to indicate evidence of a hard landing: a steel pin mounted in the upper track swivel arm and a small metal plate mounted in the lower track swivel arm of the shock absorber (Figure 1-25). The metal plate will be dented or pierced whenever the shock absorber is compressed beyond limits during a hard landing; the landing gear then has to be inspected and the plate replaced.

Nose landing gear

Hydraulically retracted and extended, locked down by a mechanical lock inside the gear actuating cylinder; a mechanical lock in the wheel well locks the gear up. It retracts aft into the fuselage, with twin nose wheels, a nose wheel steering (NWS) and damper system and wheel brakes. As the gear retracts, the wheels are automatically braked to a stop and the strut is mechanically shortened; when the gear is up and locked, brake pressure is automatically released.

Nose wheel steering

Low mode (takeoff / landing)up to 8° either side
High mode (taxiing)up to 31° either side

Directional control is obtained by operating the rudder pedals; the nose gear is controlled mechanically and operated hydraulically. Electrical power is needed to engage the high mode and simultaneously disengage the nosewheel brakes. A damper system prevents lateral oscillation of the nose wheels during takeoff, landing and taxiing. High mode is engaged by pressing the LOCK ON button, provided the flaps are up and the MRK EMERG OFF switch is in the normal (safety wired) position. If the MRK EMERG OFF switch is placed to OFF, the high steering mode cannot be activated, but the nosewheel brakes will be disabled as usual upon actuation of the LOCK ON button. When the nose gear is retracted, NWS is disconnected mechanically.

Note

Activating the high mode causes the nose wheel brakes to be disabled.

Emergency gear lowering

The pneumatic system provides compressed air to extend the landing gear, regardless of the landing gear handle position. Either the nose gear only, or nose and main gear can be extended. Pulling the EMERG GEAR handle aft directs compressed air to the nose gear hydraulic actuator to extend the nose gear; a pneumatic shut-off valve closes the hydraulic lines to prevent inadvertent gear retraction in case hydraulic pressure is regained. After the nose gear is confirmed fully extended, rotating the handle 90° clockwise and pulling full aft activates the main gear hydraulic actuators to extend the main gear. The hydraulic lines are shut off by pneumatically driven shut-off valves. Normal gear down indication on the landing signal panel is achieved after all gears are fully extended.

Note

After the landing gear has been extended with the emergency gear lowering system, normal gear retraction is not possible.

Landing gear handle: left side of the instrument panel; to move it up or down it has to be pulled to override a stop. Placing the handle in RETRACTED or EXTENDED uses DC power to actuate hydraulic valves to position the landing gear (Figure 1-25A). EMERG GEAR handle: red, beneath the left front panel. MRK EMERG OFF switch: disables the high mode of the NWS system.

Brake system

Main and nose wheels are equipped with a pneumatically operated brake system for normal operation; additional features are a run-up brake and a nose wheel brake handle to disable the nose wheel brakes if required. An emergency brake system is available for the main wheels in case of normal brake system failure.

Normal braking is accomplished by pulling the brake lever at the control stick aft; braking force is proportional to brake lever displacement. Differential braking is achieved by displacing the rudder pedals — moving the right rudder pedal forward releases brake pressure from the left main wheel brake and vice versa. For engine run-up the brake lever has to be pulled together with the run-up brake lever to achieve a higher brake force preventing the aircraft from rolling (Figure 1-26).

Caution

Under no circumstances, use the run-up brake to slow down the aircraft.

Fuse plugs

The rims of both main landing gear wheels are equipped with four fuse plugs each. Three of them, with a melting point of 126 °C ±1 °C, are mounted in the wheel flange, spaced 120° apart. If any of these fuse plugs has melted, it indicates an overheat condition of the brake system requiring a system checkout. If all three plugs have melted, the entire wheel rim must be considered damaged beyond repair. The fourth fuse plug, with a melting point of 143.5 °C ±1.5 °C, is mounted opposite the tire inflation valve. If this plug melts, the air from the tire is released completely and the brakes must be considered defective.

Anti-skid system

The wheel brake system is equipped with an electromechanical controlled anti-skid system: a wheel driven mechanical sensing unit and an electrically driven pneumatic valve per unit. The units give individual anti-skid protection to each main wheel, and to both nose wheels if either one begins to skid. The system utilizes DC power from the generator or the batteries; it is activated by placing the BAT-GND SUPPLY switch to on.

Whenever a wheel starts to skid, the wheel driven mechanical sensor closes an electrical switch, which causes the electrically driven pneumatic valve to release pneumatic air pressure from the adjacent brake. Once the wheel has regained its speed, the sensor reopens the switch and braking action is resumed.

Caution

Applying brake pressure during touchdown will cause the anti-skid system to be inoperative momentarily. Brakes should not be applied until all gears, including the nose gear, have touched down.

Emergency brake system

Pulling the emergency brake handle disables the normal braking system and directs compressed air from the pneumatic system to the main wheel brakes only. Braking action is degraded approximately 40 % compared to normal braking; differential braking is not possible. Pressure applied to the brakes is linearly proportional to the displacement of the handle; releasing the handle relieves brake pressure.

Caution

The anti-skid system is inoperative when the EMERG BRAKE handle is pulled.

Note

Emergency brakes are not to be used for normal taxiing.

11
Section 1 · pages 1-58 to 1-60

Drag chute, flaps, speedbrakes

Drag chute

A drag chute in the aft section of the fuselage between the speedbrake doors reduces landing roll distance. A red control pin is visible whenever the jaws of the attaching mechanism are open. The chute is pulled into the airstream by a pilot chute when the electrically controlled, pneumatically operated compartment door is opened. In case of main pneumatic system failure the system is buffered by a reservoir of 1.2 l (Figure 1-24). If the compartment door opens inadvertently during flight, the chute is allowed to separate from the aircraft by means of a shear bolt connecting the chute to the attaching mechanism.

Note

The drag chute will separate from the aircraft when exceeding a speed of 175 KIAS.

Operation: deployed by pressing the CHUTE DEPLOY button beneath the left canopy rail; this activates a pneumatic valve to open the compartment door, the spring-loaded pilot chute pops out and pulls out the drag chute. Jettisoned by pressing CHUTE JETTISON on the left side panel. To prevent unintentional chute release, CHUTE JETTISON is deactivated until CHUTE DEPLOY has been depressed.

Use of drag chute is mandatory for
  • Landing immediately after takeoff
  • Landing on a wet RWY
  • Short field landings
  • Landing without LEF
  • Abort after nose wheel lift off
  • Feel unit is in the position heavy

Wing flap system

Provides an automatic LEF configuration for in-flight maneuvering and a selective flap configuration for takeoff and landing. Each wing has two independent LEF, the root section consisting of three interconnected segments, and the unique end section. A single slotted flap is mounted on the trailing edge, adjacent to the fuselage. LEF and flaps are electrically selected and operated by the main hydraulic system.

The LEF incorporate hydraulic locks which lock them either in the in or out position. The flaps are locked in the up position only; the extended position depends on hydraulic pressure only, and as airspeed increases the flaps are partially blown up by the airstream.

Selective flaps

For takeoff and landing, LEF and flaps operate together. Anytime the flaps are selected down, the LEF extend automatically; if the landing gear is extended, the LEF are extended regardless of the flaps position.

Maneuvering LEF

With the flaps in the position UP, the LEF operate automatically as a function of AOA and airspeed. When the AOA is increased to 8.7° or above and the airspeed is below M 0.8+0.1−0.05, the LEF extend automatically. They retract when the AOA decreases to 7° or airspeed increases above M 0.8. The exact Mach number depends on the switching point of the mach sensor installed.

Controls (Figure 1-27): three pushbuttons on the left console — two marked FLAPS DOWN, one FLAPS UP. Pushing either FLAPS DOWN button extends all flaps; FLAPS UP retracts the flaps and LEF, provided the gear is up. The position of each flap/LEF is indicated individually by the corresponding light on the landing system signal panel (Figure 1-25).

Speedbrake system

Electrically controlled, hydraulically operated speedbrakes mounted above and beneath the drag chute compartment. The two surfaces are operated simultaneously but are not synchronized. A blow-back feature provides structural protection of the actuators and speedbrake surfaces at airspeeds above 540 KIAS.

Operated by a spring-loaded switch on the RH throttle (Figure 1-11); it returns automatically to the IN position upon release, and full extension is achieved within 3 sec. To protect the taileron operation, the speedbrakes are electrically deactivated if main or boost hydraulic pressure decreases: if boost pressure drops below 100 kp/cm² (10 MPa), the speedbrakes are retracted automatically by the main hydraulic system; if main hydraulic pressure drops below 100 kp/cm², the speedbrakes are pushed in by the air stream.

Note

Speedbrake operation is not possible with the centerline tank installed, or the gear extended. If total electrical failure occurs, the speedbrakes will retract automatically.

12
Section 1 · pages 1-61 to 1-66

Flight controls, feel and trim

Primary flight controls: tailerons, rudders and ailerons. Artificial feel systems provide simulated aerodynamic forces to control stick and rudder pedals; secondary controls are LEF, flaps and speed brakes. Mechanical linkages transmit control inputs to dual irreversible hydraulic actuators mounted next to the corresponding control surface. All primary flight controls are operated by the main and boost hydraulic system; full control command is retained if the main or boost hydraulic system fails.

Warning
  • If the emergency hydraulic pump has to be used, control will be severely degraded.
  • In order to maintain aircraft control as long as possible, flight control inputs must be smooth and kept to a minimum.

Tailerons

Longitudinal control is provided by synchronized deflection of the tailerons; partial lateral control is achieved by differential deflection.

Max pitch authority15° nose down / 35° nose up
Differential taileron± 5°
Near ground, 470–650 KTAS5°45′ ND / 17°45′ NU
Differential disabledWhen LEF extended

Taileron authority is varied as a function of airspeed and altitude; it is limited to a minimum of 5°45′ nose down and 17°45′ nose up near ground level at speeds between 470 KTAS and 650 KTAS.

Ailerons

Lateral control is provided mainly by the ailerons, assisted by the tailerons if the LEF are IN, and by the rudders at high AOA, provided the stability augmentation system is operating. Maximum aileron deflection 25° up and 15° down from the neutral position. To prevent excessive yaw during rolls, the neutral position is 5° up from the aircraft horizontal reference line; for the same reason, aileron authority is reduced above 18° AOA.

Rudders

The vertical stabilizers carry small rudders deflecting 25° to either side. The rudder feel gradient is increased by 30 kp at a rudder pedal deflection of 24 mm from the trimmed position — G: at airspeeds above M 0.8; GT: with gear up. It is strongly recommended not to override the artificial stop.

Caution

To prevent overstress of the vertical stabilizers it is prohibited to override the rudder artificial stop at airspeeds — G: >485 KIAS, GT: >432 KIAS.

Artificial feel system

Provided by a system of springs; the artificial feel applies centering forces to the stick and the rudder pedals towards the trimmed position.

Feel control unit: the pitch feel control unit uses signals from the air data computer to control an electric actuator gearbox. This gearbox varies the length of a rod by up to 50 mm, changing the stick to taileron linkage ratio, which alters the taileron deflection range and the required stick force with respect to aerodynamic forces, i.e. airspeed and altitude. The FEEL UNIT TO / LD light on the TLP illuminates whenever the feel control unit is in the easy position, e.g. during takeoff and landing (Figure 1-29).

At altitudes below 3 000 ft, the length of the variable rod depends on airspeed only: at 215 KTAS the rod starts to retract; it is fully retracted at 470 KTAS and stays fully retracted up to 650 KTAS. At 650 KTAS the rod starts to extend again and is fully extended at 810 KTAS; the FEEL UNIT TO/LD light illuminates again. At altitudes above 3 000 ft rod retraction becomes smaller with increasing altitude; above 30 000 ft it is always fully extended (Figure 1-28).

If the feel control unit fails, it can be controlled manually with the FEEL UNIT control switch on the left console — positions AUTO / OFF / EASY / HEAVY.

Warning

If the feel control unit fails, stick movements should be minimized to prevent PIOs.

Indication: AEKRAN FEEL CONT UNIT — feel control unit out of limit. VIWAS „AUSFALL ARU" / „VOR LANDUNG AUF STELLUNG LEICHT".

Roll: roll feel forces are generated by a mechanical spring unit with linear force characteristics; non-linearities are induced with the stability augmentation system engaged to provide low sensitivity for small control inputs and high sensitivity for large control inputs. Yaw: pedal feel forces are generated by a spring unit system with linear force characteristics; when the gear is retracted, a hydraulic actuator adds additional centering forces at airspeeds higher than M 0.8 and rudder pedal displacements of more than 24 mm, equivalent to 6° rudder deflection.

Trim system

Used to relieve control stick pressure; actuating a trim switch causes the appropriate trim actuator to move either in yaw, roll or pitch.

Pitch trim80 % of taileron deflection
Roll trim60 % of aileron deflection
Yaw trim60 % of rudder deflection

Pitch trim uses a trim actuator with an electric motor which varies the translation ratio of the taileron linkages, giving a new stick center position. Roll and yaw trim are likewise affected by electric motors driving the trim actuators.

Trim button unit: on the control stick grip, a pyramid cap housing two toggle switches; it provides trim control in the pitch and roll axis and is spring-loaded to the center, movable forward, aft, left and right. Rudder trim switch: on the left vertical panel (LEFT / RIGHT). Three lights on the TLP indicate the neutral position of the corresponding trim actuator.

Control stick (Figure 1-30)

  1. Gun trigger
  2. Missile trigger
  3. AP cut-out lever
  4. Brake lever
  5. Run-up brake lever
  6. CL tank jettison button
  7. Trim button
  8. Levelling button
  9. AFCS MODES OFF button
  10. Target acquisition symbol button
  11. Break-lock button
  12. Rudder pedal adjustment handle

The AFCS MODES OFF button interrupts the power supply to the automatic flight control system. The AP cut-out lever disables all automatic flight modes of the AFCS as long as it is pressed.

Rudder pedals

Conventional rudder pedals mechanically connected to hydraulic actuators. During ground operation, differential braking is controlled by the rudder pedals; they can be adjusted by the ring-type rudder adjustment handle on the control stick.

13
Section 1 · pages 1-67 to 1-70

AOA / G control system

The AOA/G control system (COC) measures and indicates angle of attack (AOA) and g-forces, controls automatic LEF operation and prevents inadvertent stalls by moving the control stick forward. Powered by 28.5 VDC and 2 phases 115 VAC.

It consists of the AOA/G computer, the combined AOA/G meter as well as warning and indicator lights, and uses inputs from the AOA vanes, Mach sensors, the g-sensor and the LEF down limit switches to:

  • Display actual and maximum g-forces
  • Display actual AOA
  • Operate the LEF automatically, considering pitch velocity
  • Compute the maximum AOA, considering LEF position and pitch rate
  • Operate the pitch kicker, considering pitch rate and AOA
  • Display system malfunctions

The g-sensor measures g-forces between −2 g and +10 g. Signals are amplified in the computer and displayed on the g-scale of the combined AOA/G meter at a rate of at least 5 g per second with an accuracy of ±0.3 g (±0.4 g under extreme weather conditions). Actual AOA is measured by the LH and RH AOA vanes from −1.5° to +29°; the computer selects the higher value and displays AOA on the AOA scale at a rate of at least 20° per second with an accuracy of ±1° (±1.5° under extreme weather conditions).

AOA limiter

The AOA/G computer uses signals from the AOA vanes and the Mach sensors to position the LEF and to actuate the pitch kicker; the system is disabled when the nose landing gear is not up and locked. The LEF extend at an AOA of 8.7° at Mach numbers below M 0.8+0.1−0.05; depending on pitch rate, the LEF may extend prior to reaching 8.7° AOA. The LEF down limit switches switch the AOA/G computer from the low AOA value of 15° (GT: 14°) maximum to the high AOA value of 26° (GT: 24°) maximum.

The pitch kicker prevents inadvertent stalls by moving the control stick forward of neutral when either pitch rate or AOA, or a combination of both, reaches the critical value. The computer triggers solenoid valves to operate the hydraulic actuators, which cause the taileron to assume an aircraft nose-down deflection and the control stick to move forward. The pilot is immediately made aware of an approaching stall condition. A force of 17 kp, in addition to normal control forces, applied on the stick can override the pitch kicker.

Note

Full aft pitch trim reduces the forward force on the control stick considerably. Under this condition, caution should be used when reapplying backstick pressure.

Caution
  • Due to extremely reduced stability margin at high AOA, an AOA reduction of approximately 4° is strongly recommended prior to initiating any roll maneuver.
  • Overriding the pitch kicker intentionally is prohibited.

System redundancy is achieved by using dual actuators operated by the main and boost hydraulic system and by duplicating the computer channels. The AOA limiter system contains continuous BIT: it monitors the heating system of the AOA vanes, AOA signal inputs and DC electrical power. The AOA vane heating system operates with reduced power when the pitot heat switch is ON, but full heating power is automatically provided when weight is off the RH main gear, regardless of switch selection. A test button on the control and test panel initiates an extended self test for maintenance purposes.

14
Section 1 · pages 1-67B to 1-72

Automatic flight control

COC indications and warnings

A complete COC failure is indicated on the TLP when both AOA limiter channels of the AOA/G computer have failed.

Caution

With a complete COC malfunction, pitch kicker warning is not available. Extreme care should be used when operating near the allowable AOA limit.

The AFCS

An electro-hydraulic system designed to provide automatic, semiautomatic and manual flying modes without interfering with the manual control. Requires DC power and 36 VAC power. It consists of the AFCS computer, the stability augmentation system, and the trim actuators (Figure FO-13).

The AFCS computer receives signals from the gyro platforms, the accelerometers, the g-meter, the control stick position and the navigation system; the signals are corrected for altitude, Mach number, AOA and pitot pressure, and processed into control signals for the dampers, the trim actuators and the flight instruments.

ModeWhat it does
DAMPERStability augmentation (pitch, roll, yaw)
ATT HOLDAttitude hold
AUTO RECOVERLevel off mode
APPROACHILS information and command steering
ALT HOLDAltitude hold
Automatic landing approach controlCombined APPROACH + ATT HOLD
LevellingAutomatic unusual attitude recovery

Swipe the table sideways →

Damper

Stability augmentation is obtained for pitch, roll and yaw by placing the AFCS switch to ON. The AFCS computer controls electro-hydraulic actuators within the mechanical control linkages to compensate any tendency of the aircraft to oscillate in roll, yaw and pitch. Aileron-rudder-interconnect is provided at high AOA by the stab aug system to improve lateral stability.

The automatic longitudinal stability control adjusts the taileron actuator to counteract pitch moments during LEF operation; it is disengaged when the LEF are in, the flaps are down or the dampers are off. The dampers are disengaged if: hydraulic supply to the actuators fails · any phase of the 200 V, 400 Hz electric power fails · the AFCS computer fails · the AFCS MODES OFF button on the control stick is pressed.

If AFCS MODES OFF is pressed less than 3 sec, the stab aug system is reengaged automatically upon release. If pressed more than 3 sec, the stab aug system disengages completely; the DAMPER pushbutton on the AFCS mode control panel must then be pressed to reengage.

Attitude hold

At bank angles from 7° to 80° and pitch angles of ±80°, the aircraft attitude is maintained. At bank angles below 7° and pitch angles of ±40°, attitude and heading are maintained. GT: at bank angles 7° to 70° and pitch angles of ±50°, the aircraft attitude is maintained.

Engaged with the ATT HOLD button on the autopilot control panel; if the damper system is off, it will automatically be engaged. The ATT HOLD light flashes until the autopilot AP cut-out lever is released; releasing the lever starts mode operation and the light becomes steady. Aircraft attitude is changed by pressing the A/P cut-out lever, attaining a new attitude and releasing the lever — stick forces have to be trimmed to balance prior to releasing the lever. Engaging attitude hold automatically disengages the levelling mode, and vice versa. Trim condition may be slightly out of balance when disengaging the mode.

Auto recover

Designed to recover the aircraft to a minimum altitude set on the radar altimeter during flights below 3 000 ft above ground level, engaged with the AUTO RECOVER pushbutton. However, engagement should not take place when flying below the preset minimum altitude. Operation is indicated by illumination of the AUTO RECOVER light.

If the aircraft descends below the preset altitude, the low altitude warning light on the radar altimeter illuminates, the AEKRAN displays ALT ALERT and VIWAS says „Gefährliche Höhe". The aircraft starts an 8° climb, initiated with 1.5 to 5.0 g. The wings are set level and the levelling button light on the control stick illuminates simultaneously. Upon reaching the preset altitude, the levelling mode is engaged automatically; when the aircraft is in level flight, ALT HOLD is engaged automatically.

If the AP cut-out lever is pressed or trim is applied during the descent, the aircraft does not recover automatically — however, the low altitude warnings are displayed and an aft stick force is applied within 3 to 4 sec. Auto recover is disengaged by pressing AUTO RECOVER again or by pressing AFCS MODES OFF for more than 3 sec; in this case the dampers disengage simultaneously and must be reengaged with the DAMPER button.

Note
  • The auto recover mode is restricted to a minimum altitude of 600 ft AGL, a max bank angle of 30° and a max descent rate of 2 000 ft per min.
  • During AUTO RECOVER, flying with the parameters mentioned above, an altitude loss of up to 300 ft has to be anticipated.

At descent rates of less than 200 ft per min with wings level, no altitude restrictions apply.

Warning

Due to radar altimeter restrictions, the AUTO RECOVER mode is not reliable at bank angles in excess of 30°.

Approach mode

Provides ILS information and command steering, engaged with the APPROACH button as soon as reliable ILS signals are received for course and glideslope. Operation is indicated by illumination of the APPROACH light and the disappearance of the pitch and course OFF-flags on the ADI.

Caution

To prevent (violent) control transients, the AFCS mode ATT HOLD must be disengaged prior to engagement of the APPROACH mode.

Bank and pitch commands are provided by the course and pitch steering bar on the ADI and the command circle in the HUD. Bank steering commands are based on a roll rate of 5 to 8° per sec. The pitch steering bar provides steering towards the engagement altitude of the APPROACH mode until glide path interception. Centering the pitch and course steering bar, as shown by the command circle in the HUD, ensures proper steering. Failure of the glide slope indication causes a level-off command by the pitch steering bar on the ADI; the pitch OFF-flag on the ADI and the ILS glide slope OFF-flag on the HSI will appear.

Warning

When any OFF-flag on HSI or ADI appears, level off immediately and execute a missed approach.

Approach mode can be deselected by pressing the AFCS MODES OFF button for less than 3 sec.

Altitude hold

Maintains the aircraft at a specific barometric altitude. Engaged by pressing ATT HOLD first and then ALT HOLD; illumination of both lights indicates proper operation. To engage, the pitch attitude must not exceed ±5° — if it does, the aircraft stabilizes at the given angle and the ALT HOLD light flashes until the angle is decreased below 5°. After correction to the engagement altitude, the aircraft is stabilized in bank angle and altitude; if the bank angle was less than 7° during engagement, heading and altitude are stabilized.

Altitude hold can be cut out intermittently by pressing the AP cut-out lever, indicated by flashing of the ATT HOLD and ALT HOLD lights. Pressing AFCS MODES OFF for less than 3 sec disengages the altitude hold mode. After recovery to level flight with the levelling mode, ALT HOLD is engaged automatically.

Note
  • Altimeter fluctuations while accelerating through the transonic range will produce transient fluctuations, which, although not violent, may cause the reference altitude to slip.
  • Do not use ALT HOLD at altitudes below 300 ft AGL.

Automatic landing approach control

Can be engaged after the approach mode has been selected and the pitch and course steering bars on the ADI have been centered. For smooth operation, airspeed should be below 215 KIAS. Automatic throttle adjustment is not available.

To engage, the ATT HOLD button has to be pressed in addition to the APPROACH button. Illumination of the ATT HOLD and the ALT HOLD lights as well as the disappearance of the OFF-flags on the ADI/HSI indicate proper system operation. Level flight is maintained until glide slope interception; upon glide slope interception, the ALT HOLD light extinguishes and the aircraft begins the descent. Course corrections are performed with bank angles up to 5°, glide slope corrections with pitch angles up to 2°.

The automatic landing approach system can be temporarily disengaged by pressing the A/P cut-out lever and is automatically reengaged as soon as this lever is released. It has to be discontinued if the pitch or course steering bar on the ADI indicate a difference to the course or glide slope indication on the HSI, or the minimum altitude of 150 ft is reached. It is disengaged by pressing AFCS MODES OFF for less than 3 sec or by engaging the AFCS levelling mode.

Warning

The autopilot may trim the aircraft considerably out of balance. Therefore, when disengaging the automatic landing approach mode, be prepared to counteract large control transients.

Levelling mode

Recovers the aircraft to straight and level flight in case of pilot's spatial disorientation. Pressing the levelling button on the right side of the trim button disengages all other AFCS modes and engages the levelling mode, provided the AP cut-out lever is released. If the dampers are OFF, they are automatically engaged. Levelling operation is indicated by steady illumination of the button light.

At bank angles below 80°, bank and pitch attitude are recovered to level flight simultaneously. At bank angles of more than 80° bank is recovered to below 80° before simultaneous recovery. The recovery rate varies from 10° to 45° per sec in bank and −1 g to +5 g in pitch, depending on altitude, attitude and airspeed.

Once the aircraft is recovered to ±7° AOB and ±5° of pitch or below, the ALT HOLD mode is automatically engaged within 3 to 4 sec, as indicated by the ALT HOLD light. If the pilot interferes during levelling operations by pressing the AP cut-out lever or using the trim button, the levelling mode disengages momentarily, indicated by flashing of the levelling light. Levelling mode is disengaged either by pressing AFCS MODES OFF for less than 3 sec, or by engaging the attitude hold mode.

Note
  • During levelling operations, the rudder pedals must be neutralized and maintained in neutral position.
  • Throttle adjustments may be required according to airspeed and altitude.
  • If a forward trim condition exists prior to engagement of levelling, negative g may be experienced momentarily before positive recovery.
  • During recovery from negative pitch angles, or bank angles of 40° to 50°, bank may increase up to 70°, not resulting in additional loss of altitude.

AFCS BITE

Placing the AFCS switch to ON initiates the BIT, provided weight is on the nose gear, the inertial platforms are ready and hydraulic pressure is available. Prior to engagement, the control surfaces must be trimmed to neutral, as shown by the indicator lights.

During the BIT, controls must be released to allow unrestricted movements. The DAMPER OFF light illuminates on the TLP and the MASTER CAUTION light flashes; the DAMPER light flashes continuously at a rate of 1.5 to 2.0 cycles per second and all other lights on the AFCS control panel may illuminate temporarily, except for the MISSED APPROACH light.

Upon completion of the BIT, the DAMPER OFF light on the TLP extinguishes and the DAMPER light illuminates steadily, indicating satisfactory BIT completion and the stab aug system engaged. If the control stick is out of the neutral position it must be trimmed back to neutral.

An AFCS malfunction is indicated by flashing of all lights on the AFCS control panel, except for the MISSED APPROACH light. If the malfunction is not within the stab aug system, the dampers can be engaged by pushing the DAMPER button; in this case only the damper function is usable, none of the other AFCS modes may be engaged.

A normal test cycle lasts 90 sec. However, the dampers can be engaged after 40 sec; in this case the BIT is interrupted and none of the other AFCS modes can be engaged. After neutralizing the control stick the BIT may be reinitiated by pressing the AFCS MODES OFF button momentarily.

Note

With the ICAO II modification implemented, the course pointer must be set to a vertical position before the AFCS self test is initiated.

Controls

AFCS switch on the system power panel (Figure 1-31) switches the AFCS ON and OFF. AFCS control panel in front of the left console has five pushbuttons — DAMPER, AUTO RECOVER, ALT HOLD, ATT HOLD, APPROACH, MISSED APPROACH — and when a mode is selected the corresponding green light illuminates. The MISSED APPROACH button is used to obtain steering information from the navigation system. AP cut-out lever integrated into the control stick grip disables the AFCS flying modes while pressed; the associated AFCS modes indicator lights begin to flash. AFCS MODES OFF button on the left side of the trim button disengages all AFCS modes; the stab aug system will be reengaged if pressed for less than 3 sec, and if pressed for more than 3 sec the system is switched off and the DAMPER OFF light on the TLP illuminates — the AFCS is disengaged completely. Levelling button with integrated indicator light to the right side of the trim button engages the unusual attitude recovery mode.

Warning

When an AFCS mode is selected, be prepared to manually counteract any abrupt control movements in the event of an AFCS malfunction.

15
Section 1 · pages 1-73 to 1-75

Pitot static and air data

Pitot static system

Two pitot booms, a main and an emergency pitot boom, supply impact and static pressures to various flight instruments and aneroid switches (Figure 1-32). The main pitot boom provides pressure to the IAS/TAS indicator, the VVI, the ADC and the IFF. The emergency pitot boom provides pressure for the Mach transducer, the LEF controls, the ECU, the AFCS, the engine intake ramp control and the ejection seat. If the main system fails, the emergency pitot boom can be selected to provide pressure to the main system users.

Pitot selector lever: on the pedestal panel, positions MAIN and STBY. Pitot heat switch: on the RH side wall; it controls the heating elements in both pitot booms, AOA probes and the windshield. Heating elements are energized any time 28 VDC power is available and the pitot heat switch is ON; AOA probe and windshield heater elements are energized when weight is off the wheels and 115 VAC / 400 Hz power is available.

Caution

Pitot heat should not be used for more than one minute during ground operations to prevent damage to the system.

Air data computer

Part of the pitot static system and consists of the air data system, the pressure altimeter and the TAS indicator. It uses inputs of pitot and static pressure from the main pitot system and OAT, and provides electrical outputs representing TAS, Mach number, pressure altitude and density altitude. Data are supplied to the navigation system, the AFCS, the fire control system and the fuel indication system. The ADC uses DC power from the generator or the batteries, 36 VAC and 115 VAC. A build in test is provided to check system readiness during preflight preparation and checkout for maintenance purpose.

Indication: AEKRAN AIR DATA SYS — unreliability of airspeed, altitude and vertical velocity. VIWAS „AUSFALL SWS" / „AP AUS, Vmax 600".

16
Section 1 · pages 1-76 to 1-83

Instruments and displays

IAS indicator (USM-2AE)

A single pointer indicates airspeed values between 0 and 800 kts on a non-linear scale; Mach number is indicated on the inner scale. Pneumatic inputs are impact and static pressure supplied by the main or the backup pitot tube.

Note

Since the indicator is directly driven by the pneumatic outputs of one of the pitot tubes, the indicated Mach number may differ from the real value by as much as M 0.05 due to non-linearities of those pitot tubes.

TAS indicator (UMS-2.5-2U)

Combined display of TAS and Mach number. Electrical power is supplied from the ADC since it is part of the system. The longer pointer rotates at the outer scale to indicate values between 100 and 1 400 kts; the shorter pointer traverses the inner Mach number scale. Input signals are supplied by the ADC and the ambient air temperature sensor.

GT rear cockpit: the TAS indicator UIS-1250 AE provides the display of true airspeed between 100 and 1 250 kts.

Altimeter

An electrically operated instrument indicating from 0 to 100 000 ft. Electrical power is supplied by the ADC system, since the altimeter is an integral part of this system. An adjustable barometric scale allows the altimeter to be set at the corrected sea level pressure.

GT rear cockpit: a pneumatically operated instrument indicating 0 to 100 000 ft, incorporating a vibrator which reduces mechanical friction of gear trains and linkages; the vibrator is powered by 28.5 VDC from the generator, or in case of failure by the batteries. A barometric setting knob adjusts the setting on the hPa counter between 700 and 1 080 hPa.

Combined AOA / G meter

A combined instrument with two different indicating systems; since it is part of the COC, it receives electrical power via this system. The AOA pointer moving along the left scale is electrically connected to AOA probes at the left and right forward section of the aircraft.

G-loads are indicated on the right scale by a main pointer indicating instantaneous g-loads and an index tab driven by the main pointer; the index tab remains on its maximum indication until reset. The g meter is electrically connected to an external g-sensing transducer.

Face markings: reset button for the G-index tab · AOA pointer · 15° marker (red) · red region · 5.7 G-index (red) · max G-index tab · G pointer.

Attitude director indicator

Pictorial display of the aircraft's attitude in pitch, roll and turn, using 36 VAC and 28.5 VDC from the gyro system. A slip indicator is integrated at the bottom part. Attitude is indicated by the aircraft symbol in relation to the horizon, pitch by the attitude sphere.

Callouts: 1 gyro cage button / gyro fail light · 2 glide slope deviation indicator · 3 pitch steering bar · 4 pitch OFF flag · 5 course deviation indicator · 6 azimuth OFF flag · 7 attitude sphere · 8 center dot · 9 aircraft symbol · 10 bank scale · 11 aircraft symbol setting knob · 12 slip indicator · 13 course steering bar.

Pitch and bank: pitch is displayed by the pitch scale on the spheroid surface and the center of the aircraft symbol, whose vertical position can be adjusted with the setting knob. Bank angle is displayed by the aircraft symbol rolling on the spheroid surface on the bank scale. Slip is indicated by a ball inside a tubular case at the lower part of the instrument.

Glide slope deviation indicator: during NAV mode RETURN, a 7° glide slope is displayed for extended runway centerline interception at 2 000 ft AGL. During NAV mode MISSED APPROACH, deviation from an altitude of 2 000 ft AGL is displayed; in AFCS mode LANDING, deviation from the ILS glide path is displayed. Course deviation indicator: during NAV modes RETURN and MISSED APPROACH the index provides steering for extended runway centerline intercept; in AFCS mode LANDING, deviation from the ILS course is displayed.

Command steering: during an ILS approach with AFCS mode APPROACH selected, command steering information is available by the pitch steering bar and the bank steering bar. When the aircraft is exactly on the desired flight path, the intersection of the two bars coincides with the center dot; the bars are parked in the center when the system is not engaged, but the pitch and azimuth OFF flags will be visible.

OFF flags: two red flags in the upper left and right part — pitch OFF flag marked T and azimuth OFF flag marked K — visible whenever either channel of the ILS system has failed or is not activated. As soon as AFCS mode APPROACH is selected and no malfunctions exist, both OFF flags disappear.

Note

During an automatic landing approach, the appearance of either OFF flag initiates an automatic level off by the AFCS.

Horizontal situation indicator

Provides a horizontal view of the aircraft with respect to the navigation situation; the compass card rotates so that the aircraft heading is always under the course index. Three OFF flags provide warnings for course and glide path indicator failures or navigation or gyro/plateform malfunctions. Depending on the selection on the NAV panel, indications on the HSI vary. Utilizes 36 VAC.

Callouts: 1 test button · 2 fixed compass card · 3 ILS course OFF flag · 4 bearing pointer (yellow) · 5 course pointer (white) · 6 range counter · 7 HSI OFF flag · 8 course index · 9 BRG counter · 10 ILS glide slope indicator · 11 ILS course deviation scale · 12 ILS glide slope OFF flag · 13 compass card · 14 course selector knob · 15 ILS glide slope deviation scale · 16 ILS course deviation indicator.

Vertical velocity indicator and clock

The VVI indicates the rate of climb or descent, connected to the static pressure system; pointer actuation is controlled by the rate of change of atmospheric pressure. It registers a rate of gain or loss of altitude too small to cause a noticeable change in the altimeter reading. A turn and slip indicator is incorporated: the turn needle indicates direction of turn but does not provide accurate turn rate. Receives 3 phases 36 VAC from the gyro system.

Clock: a mechanical clock for normal daytime, elapsed (mission) time, with a stopwatch feature, read on three scales — normal daytime on the outer scale with hour and minute pointer; elapsed time in hours and minutes on the upper inner scale; elapsed time in minutes and seconds (stopwatch) on the lower inner scale. A red winding and setting knob at the lower left corner winds the clock counter-clockwise and, when pulled, permits setting. Pushing the knob starts the small elapsed time scale (a status window changes white to red); pushing again stops it (indicators turn red/white); a third push resets the elapsed time and the status indicator turns white. A setting knob at the lower right corner starts and stops the seconds pointer of the normal daytime scale and operates the stopwatch.

Radar altimeter

The continuous wave radar altimeter measures height above surface and supplies information to the avionics equipment and the radar altimeter indicator. The height marker may be set to the desired minimum height; if the aircraft is below this height, the radar altimeter forwards inputs to AFCS, AEKRAN, VIWAS and the RAD ALT indicator warning light. Accuracy of the minimum height selected is 1.5 ft from 0 to 60 ft and ±3 % above 60 ft.

Switched on with the ACFT SYS switch; after the warm-up period the indicator OFF flag disappears and an altitude of 0 ±3 ft is indicated. It contains continuous BIT and is powered by 28.5 VDC and 115 VAC — if the DC generator fails, power is supplied from the aircraft batteries, and if the AC generator fails, from the PTO.

The system provides height information from 0 to 3 000 ft AGL within bank angles up to 15°. Accuracy: ±3 ft from 0 to 30 ft, ±10 % above 30 ft. At heights above 3 000 ft an OFF flag appears on the indicator and the pointer rotates to the black sector; identical indications occur with a malfunction. A test button moves the pointer to the test mark at 45 ft.

Warning

At bank angles above 30° or over rough terrain, RAD ALT may give false height information. At bank angles from 15° to 30° system accuracy decreases; above 30° bank it should be considered unreliable.

Indication: AEKRAN ALT ALERT — descent below set minimum height. VIWAS „GEFÄHRLICHE HÖHE".

HUD / HDD

Consists of the head up display, the head down display, units for image processing, synchronization and power supply. Powered by 28.5 VDC and 115/200 VAC. It displays information originating from the navigation system and the fire control system; signals from the AFCS, AOA and side slip vanes, and from the radar altimeter are processed.

HUD: projects information in symbolic and numeric form into the pilot's field of view — the primary source of information providing steering commands in the navigation mode and the primary source of information during the attack phase. The image processing unit receives inputs from the navigation system, the FCS and additionally from the AFCS, AOA and sideslip vanes and the radar altimeter; it generates symbols displayed on a CRT and projected into the pilot's line of sight by a collimator and a combining glass. The collimator focuses the HUD picture to infinity.

The combining glass projects the symbology within a space of 13° in azimuth and 18° in elevation, resulting in a circular field of view of 24°. A light filter may be raised to ensure readability of the HUD display against a bright background; the filter operating handle on top of the left mirror unit of the helmet mounted sight erects the filter to the vertical position.

HDD: a TV monitor on the right side of the instrument panel displaying essentially the same picture as the HUD. An LDR in the lower right corner of the front panel automatically adjusts brightness; in combination with the CRT brightness control knob it renders the information readable even in direct sunlight.

Section 1 · pages 1-84 to 1-85

Canopy

The canopy consists of a rigid curved front section, the windshield, fixed to the fuselage, and a section that can be raised, hinged aft. Normal canopy operation is controlled by the canopy control handle and powered by the pneumatic power supply system (Figure 1-49).

The pneumatic canopy operation system ensures raising and lowering of the canopy corresponding to the control handle position, downlock of the canopy in the closed position, and sealing of the canopy.

Internal canopy control handle — three position detents: Open, taxi, and closed. To open the canopy, first set the handle in the taxi position and then in the open position. When the handle is in the taxi position, the seal is deflated and the canopy is released and lifted approximately two inches above the cockpit rim. Moving the handle further into the open position, the canopy is raised and held by a pneumatic actuator.

Caution
  • Taxiing with the canopy in the open position is prohibited.
  • Max speed for taxiing is 16 kts with the canopy in taxi position.

GT: identical internal control handles are located in both cockpits; the rear cockpit canopy control handle is safety wired to the close position, since normal canopy operation is performed from the front cockpit. Opening the rear handle to the taxi or open position overrides the front cockpit handle and positions it accordingly; when either handle is moved from the open position towards the taxi or closed position, the other handle is automatically positioned accordingly.

External canopy operating handle — mechanically linked to the internal handle and located on the LH front fuselage; used to open or close the canopy from the outside.

Operation without pneumatic pressure: set the control handle to the open position to disengage the locks, then raise the canopy manually and hold it in the open position with the canopy retaining rod.

Canopy jettison: the emergency jettison system provides release and separation from the cockpit if the emergency jettison handle on the right cockpit sill is pulled, or automatically if ejection is initiated. A pyro-mechanical system is used; explosive cartridges open the locks. GT: emergency jettison handles are located in both cockpits on the right cockpit sill — pulling either handle jettisons the canopy.

Section 1 · pages 1-86 to 1-90

Ejection seat K-36 DM

The K-36 DM provides safe escape from the aircraft under various combinations of aircraft altitude, speed, attitude and flight path. The seat is propelled from the aircraft by a cartridge-operated twin barrel ejection gun assisted by a rocket motor, both at the back of the seat. The system functions at all altitudes at speeds up to 700 kts; during ground operation a minimum of 40 kts (80 kts for the trainer version) is required for safe canopy separation.

Pulling the ejection handle initiates the sequence, causing the canopy to be jettisoned and the ejection gun to fire. Maintain a continuous pull until full travel of the handle is reached and the seat fires. The sequence continues until a normal parachute descent is accomplished; after the initial firing of the seat, seat operation is completely automatic and requires no additional action by the occupant.

Note

Canopy jettison malfunctions will not interfere with the seat firing system. Should the canopy fail to jettison after ejection has been initiated, the seat fires through the canopy after a delay of 1 sec.

Warning

The escape system is a potential source of danger and inadvertent operation may cause fatal injuries. Upon completion of the flight, the pilot must ensure that the seat is in the 'safe for parking' condition. Safety pins are provided to various components of the escape system (Figure FO-18).

Ejection sequence (Figure 1-50)

The sequence is electrically controlled until firing of the ejection gun; a mechanical backup provides fail-safe operation. As the main cartridge of the pyro-mechanical system is fired, gases are ducted to the canopy lock-down mechanism to jettison the canopy, to retract and lock the shoulder harness and lap belt by means of retraction units, and to activate both leg raisers and arm protectors.

Simultaneously a backup system is activated to open the canopy locks after 0.5 sec in case of a main breech unit failure; it allows the seat to fire through the canopy after another 0.5 sec.

As the canopy is jettisoned, the canopy firing cable is pulled, allowing the twin barrel ejection gun to fire and accelerate to at least 13.6 m/s. As the seat rises along the cockpit rails, the emergency oxygen supply is tripped, a body windshield is activated above 485 kts, and the leg restraint lines are retracted. The rocket motor fires to propel the seat to a greater height. The seat is stabilized and decelerated by two rotating drogues on telescopic struts during descent through the upper atmosphere with the occupant securely restrained in the seat.

Automatic operation of the delay-release mechanism occurs after reaching the barostat altitude (16 000 ft), or in ejections below this altitude, when the seat is decelerated to parachute-opening speed. The headrest / parachute container is fired from the seat to pull out the parachute; the recoil produced is also used during man / seat separation.

Sequence timing

Ejection gun development0.2 sec
Initiator cable fired at104.5–107.5 cm rail travel
First barostat delay unit16 000 ft MSL / 19 500 ft (mountainous)
…time release4 sec
Second barostat delay unit6 500 ft MSL / 10 000 ft (mountainous)
…time release0.7 sec
Below 6 500 ft, readjusted0.1 sec at 375 KTAS → 1.75 sec at 750 KTAS

Drogue chute area 0.06 m², ribbon-type with opposite direction of rotation to stabilize the seat. Rocket motor thrust 3 300 kg. Personal parachute 60 m² packed in the headrest container.

Seat components

  • Ejection gun: a single percussion-fired cartridge gun of three major assemblies — breech firing mechanism, fillet transition piece and telescopic launch tube. Mounted to the seat structure except for the inner barrel of the launch tube, which is mounted to the bulkhead of the cockpit. After ignition it develops thrust for 0.2 sec.
  • Rocket motor: located under the seat pan, ignited as the seat leaves the ejection gun by a static line which cocks and triggers a firing pin. Develops a thrust of 3 300 kg.
  • Drogue gun: two drogue arms on the right and left side of the headrest, with firing mechanism and telescopic rod with built-in drogue chute. Triggered as the seat raises along the guide rails; cartridge gas extends each rod aft at an angle of 15° and deploys the drogue chute.
  • Delay unit: two independent time release mechanisms installed to the right and left side of the main beam assembly, to delay deployment of the personal parachute and separation of the occupant from the seat until it has descended from high altitude and/or slowed enough to prevent excessive opening shock. Both units operate independently but each triggers the parachute deployment mechanism of both units.
  • Harness powered retraction unit: a powered inertia lock providing a velocity (g-sensing) system and a power retraction system. The inertia lock provides safe restraint during violent manoeuvres (g-sensing mechanism in accordance with acceleration, 2 g); manual locking can be accomplished by the shoulder harness release handle on the left forward side of the seat bucket.
  • Lap retraction unit: a safe hold in the seat during normal flight, manually adjustable with the lap adjustment lever on the right side of the seat bucket; gas-powered retraction is automatically activated when the ejection handle is pulled.
  • Arm protection system: two metal blades mounted to the side of the backrest, rotated down to a horizontal position at ejection to prevent flailing injuries to the arms.
  • Windshield: two telescopic rods that extend and raise a shield of Kopran ribbons in front of the pilot, designed to extend even when one rod fails. Activated above 485 KTAS and raised by an electro-pyrotechnic charge.
  • Leg restraint lines: routed along the cockpit sidewall, the instrument panel and the control stick casing, fixed into position with clips; padding is fitted where they retract the legs. On ejection the legs are firmly pulled against the seat bucket and the thighs lifted to optimize body position.
  • Emergency oxygen system: a bottle in the seat bucket, activated automatically on ejection or manually by pulling the emergency knob (red mushroom) on the right side of the seat bucket — once pulled it cannot be shut off. Contains 0.7 l of compressed oxygen at 180 kp/cm², supplying 100 % oxygen for about 6 min during emergency descent, 3 to 4 min during high altitude ejection and 3 min at low altitude.
  • Seat position switch: the seat may be adjusted vertically only, by a momentary contact switch on the right side of the seat bucket, through a total range of 135 mm. It is not necessary to adjust seat height before ejection.
  • Survival pack: survival equipment, emergency locator beacon, emergency ration, first aid kit and distress signalling kit, stored in the seat pan beside the dinghy, covered by a cushioned profile seating face. Released automatically after man / seat separation, inflating the floating device of the locator beacon and the dinghy automatically. If the dinghy fails to unfold before landing it can be inflated manually by a handle on the CO₂ bottle; if the locator beacon float fails to inflate completely it can be inflated manually.

Dual ejection (GT): as soon as either the F/C or the R/C ejection handle is pulled, the ejection sequence starts. The rear seat always ejects first, followed by the front seat after 1 sec.

19
Section 1 · pages 1-90A to 1-92

Air conditioning and pressurization

Two major systems — one for the cockpit and one for electronic equipment compartments (Figure FO-14). The cockpit air is conditioned to a defined temperature and pressure; the avionics air conditioning system provides cooled air for the various equipment compartments.

Engine bleed air for both systems passes through a common line to a pair of identical pressure reducer valves, arranged in series for fail-safe operation. It is routed through a parallel arrangement of two air-air coolers and an evaporator cooler; behind the evaporator cooler the airstream is divided for equipment cooling and cockpit air conditioning. The air for equipment cooling passes through a turbo cooler, and as a cooling medium through a heat exchanger / dehumidifier for the cockpit air before being supplied to the equipment compartments.

The air for the cockpit is passed through the heat exchanger / dehumidifier and cooled down in a second turbo cooler; after being mixed with hot air from the pressure reducer valves it enters the cockpit through several manifolds. Hot bleed air used for windshield defogging is taken from the pressure reducer valves and routed to a motor driven valve which remains open at airspeeds below M 0.8.

Cabin temperature control

The temperature of the air supplied to the cockpit and/or canopy is regulated by regulating the mixing ratio of cold and hot air; normally the ratio is adjusted automatically to maintain the selected cockpit temperature, but manual adjustment is possible. DC power is required for temperature control.

CABIN TEMP switchFunction
AUTOCockpit temperature automatically adjusted in accordance with the setting of the cabin temperature control knob on the main vertical console
Center positionNeutral; removes electrical supply from the mixing valve, freezing it in its last position
HOT / COLDMixing valve driven in the appropriate direction; the switch should only be bumped to the position momentarily to prevent the valve from driving to an extreme temperature position

Swipe the table sideways →

Cabin pressurization — MiG-29G

Controlled by a cabin pressure control valve. When the aircraft is below 6 500 ft, the control valve automatically maintains a pressure difference of 0.05 kp/cm² (50 hPa) or less. From 6 500 ft up, differential pressure increases up to 40 000 ft: the differential pressure of 0.29 to 0.31 kp/cm² (300 ±10 % hPa) obtained between 30 000 and 40 000 ft is maintained constant at higher altitudes (Figure 1-51).

A safety relieve valve controls cabin pressure at a nominal 0.33 kp/cm² (33 kPa) above ambient pressure in case the cabin pressure control valve fails. If ambient pressure exceeds cabin pressure, a vacuum valve opens to allow pressure compensation.

Cabin pressurization — MiG-29GT

Prior to takeoff and immediately after landing the cockpit is not pressurized. In flight the cockpit is pressurized to a cockpit altitude equivalent to an altitude below mean sea level immediately after takeoff. As altitude increases, differential pressure increases so that a cockpit altitude equivalent to mean sea level is maintained up to approximately 4 000 ft. From 4 000 ft up the pressure differential increases continuously until a differential pressure of 290 hPa is reached at 12 000 ft MSL; above 12 000 ft a differential pressure of 290 hPa is maintained (Figure 1-51A). A safety relieve valve controls cabin pressure at a nominal 315 to 340 hPa above ambient pressure.

Windshield defogging

Fogging of the windshield is prevented by heating the inside surface of the glass with hot air; air from the pressure reducer valve is delivered through defogging manifolds at airspeeds below M 0.8. Cold air is automatically mixed with the hot air to prevent inconvenient cockpit temperature. When the mixing valve is fully open, windshield defogging is automatically shut off to prevent an overtemperature; manual shut down is possible with the CABIN AIR lever.

Anti-G valve and vent suit valve

The anti g valve controls air delivery to the anti g suit; air is tapped from downstream of the air-air coolers, passed through a regulator valve, an anti g valve, and delivered to the suit via the PEC. Below 2.5 g no pressure passes through the suit; above 2.5 g the valve controls the suit pressure in proportion to the g-forces experienced.

Note

For proper inflation of the anti g suit, the pressure regulator must be set to min. Any position other than min will result in premature pressurization.

The ventilation suit valve controls air delivery to a ventilation suit; air is tapped from downstream of the turbo cooler, passed through an ejector valve and mixed with hot air, and delivered via the PEC.

Section 1 · pages 1-94 to 1-96

External lighting and oxygen

External lighting

Navigation lights, anti collision lights, landing and taxi lights; all external lights are powered by the DC system.

Navigation lights: two position lights at the wing tips — green right, red left — and a white one at the left vertical stabilizer. Controlled by the NAV LTS switch on the forward lighting control panel, modes OFF, 100 %, 10 % and FLASH. On the ground the navigation lights are in the 10 % intensity mode regardless of mode switch setting.

Anti collision lights: installed behind the cockpit and on the left engine bay, controlled by the ANTI COLL switch.

Landing / taxi lights: two landing lights, one on each main landing gear door, and a single taxi light on the nosewheel strut. The right landing light beam is angled down 10° with respect to the horizon and offset by 12° to the left with respect to the aircraft's center line; the left landing light beam is angled down 8° and offset 14° left. The taxi light beam is aligned parallel to the horizon and to the center line. With the switch in TAXI only the taxi light is on; in LAND both taxi and landing lights are on. Landing lights are disabled when the gear is retracted, regardless of switch position.

Internal lighting

Console panel lights, instrument lights, console flood lights, spot lights, map reading light and associated controls. The control panels and indicators are powered by the AC system, the console floodlights for panels, instruments and the map reading light by the DC system. Instruments are illuminated with shielded light fixtures located adjacent to each indicator; the major left and right console control panels are indirectly illuminated.

  • PANEL control knob — dual function: pushed in, manual intensity control of all cockpit information and warning lights except AEKRAN; pulled out, intensity is automatically controlled by a photo diode according to ambient brightness.
  • MAP ILLUM control knob — switches and dims the map reading light located near this panel.
  • INSTRUMENT control knob — switches and dims the instrument illumination.
  • CONSOLE control knob — switches and controls the intensity of the indirect illumination of various switches and control knobs.
  • Two further control knobs on the forward lighting control panel control the floodlights and the brightness of the landing system signal panel illumination.

Oxygen system

A pressure demand system, consisting of a main system located in the fuselage, an engine supply system and an emergency system on the ejection seat (Figure FO-15). Oxygen supply for the main system and the engine supply is replenished through one single charging connection; emergency oxygen supply is charged directly to the bottle. The system is mechanically controlled, however 115 VAC is required for indicator operation.

Main system: three 4 litre high pressure gaseous oxygen bottles (MiG-29GT: seven bottles), charged at 150 kp/cm²; further components are an oxygen flow valve, a pressure reduction valve, an oxygen flow regulator, a PEC, a pressure regulator, the combined oxygen indicator and the oxygen control panel.

Oxygen controls (Figure 1-54)

ControlFunction
OXYGEN FLOW valve (LH console)Rotary knob marked OPEN / CLOSED — controls the supply of oxygen to the system
MIX – 100 % switch (blue)Selects either an oxygen / air mixture or pure oxygen
EMERGENCY ON – OFF switch (red)Selects 100 % oxygen with positive pressure or normal oxygen supply. Should remain in OFF at all times unless an unscheduled pressure increase is required. In EMERGENCY ON, 100 % oxygen is provided with continuous positive pressure to the face mask
HELM VENT ON – OFF switch (black)Activates the helmet ventilation system

Swipe the table sideways →

Note

When EMERGENCY ON is selected, use of oxygen is 2 to 3 times higher than normal. Quantity remaining must be continuously monitored.

Oxygen pressure regulator: comprises an airmix and a 100 % oxygen demand type regulator. With MIX selected, the air / oxygen ratio is determined by an air inlet valve and varies according to cabin altitude: below 6 600 ft pure cabin air is delivered; above 6 600 ft the air inlet valve reduces the air percentage until 100 % oxygen is delivered at 26 000 ft; above 40 000 ft pressure breathing is introduced with pressure increasing with altitude. Between 0 and 40 000 ft with 100 % selected, the 100 % regulator delivers 100 % oxygen; above that level, pressure breathing is introduced with pressure increasing with altitude.

Combined oxygen indicator (Figure 1-55)

Center of the front panel; three thermometer-type scales with triangular pointers and one rectangular pointer for oxygen flow:

  • Cabin altitude — scale calibrated in km; as long as the cabin is not pressurized, the pointer indicates actual flight altitude.
  • Oxygen quantity — 100 % is indicated with a pressure of 150 kp/cm² in the oxygen bottles; as pressure decreases, indication drops proportionally.
  • Oxygen flow — during normal flow the pointer moves up during inhalation and down during exhalation; a steady pointer indicates no oxygen is supplied (e.g. with MIX selected at low altitude).
  • Cabin pressure differential — utmost right scale.

Indication: AEKRAN EMERG OXYGEN RESERVE — oxygen quantity 15 %; VIWAS „SAUERSTOFFVORRAT MINIMAL".

Communications, recorders

Antenna system (Figure 1-56)

Radar · IRSTS · TACAN · ADF · RHAW · UHF/VHF radio · XT-2000 · IFF/SIF · RAD ALT · marker beacon · (item 11 not used).

VHF / UHF radio

Voice communication is provided by the VHF/UHF radio: 2 000 VHF and 7 200 UHF frequencies can be used, 29 preset frequencies are available, with UHF guard channel monitoring. Power to operate the radio is supplied by the DC generator or the batteries; the RADIO switch is on the right console.

Note

Due to the wide-band antenna location in the right fin-tip, communication may be interrupted momentarily during turns exceeding 45° AOB.

Frequency control panel (LH console, Figure 1-57): ADF switch · GUARD RCVR switch · SQLCH switch · PRESET / MANUAL rotary switch · five frequency toggle switches (VHF ×2, UHF ×3).

Radio panel (LH console): volume control knob · guard receiver select switch · squelch switch · guard receiver control light (illuminates when guard transmissions are received even if the guard receiver is deselected) · ADF switch (transmissions on the selected ADF frequency can be monitored).

Indicator control panel (Figure 1-58): channel selector knob (29 preset frequencies) · channel display · frequency display · DIM knob · STORE pushbutton.

With the preset / manual switch on MAN, five toggle switches select the desired frequency: physically 100.000 to 399.975 MHz in increments of 0.025 MHz, but only 100.000–149.975 MHz and 220.000–399.975 MHz can be used. The last digit (0 or 5) is not displayed; if an unusable frequency is selected the indication flashes. Manual entry uses a six-digit frequency; the last two digits (00-25-50-75) are selected with one toggle switch. In PRE, select the desired channel with the channel selector knob; to change a stored frequency, select the channel, insert the new frequency via the toggle switches, press STORE.

Transmission is accomplished by pressing the throttle-mounted microphone button; receiver signal is controlled with the volume knob on the control panel.

Emergency UHF radio (XT-2000)

Provides air-to-air and air-to-ground communication on the UHF preset distress frequency of 243.0 MHz and two further preset channels; it can also be used as guard or auxiliary receiver in the airborne communication system. Powered by 28.5 VDC and utilizes the emergency UHF antenna in the left vertical fin. Control panel on the forward LH console (Figure 1-59): function selector (OFF / R receive only / T/R transmit and receive) · volume control knob · channel selector (1, 2, G — G selects 243.0 MHz guard) · test pushbutton · test indicator light.

Built-in test: function selector T/R · channel selector to desired channel · press and hold test pushbutton. The indicator light illuminates as long as the pushbutton is held, and a short tone is heard if the system is operating properly. If there is a system malfunction the indicator light flashes momentarily and then extinguishes, and the audio tone is not heard.

Operation: as guard or auxiliary receiver — function selector R, channel selector to desired channel, press test pushbutton, volume control to desired audio level. As transmitter / receiver — function selector T/R, channel to desired channel, test pushbutton pressed, volume to desired level, PTT button pressed for transmission.

Intercom system

Enables communication between the ground crew and the pilot (GT: additionally between the two cockpits). All audio warnings produced by various aircraft systems and identification signals from radio and navigation equipment are routed to the pilot's headset; volume of the radio and navigation equipment is adjusted by the relevant volume control. Aircraft warnings are transmitted at an audio level high enough to attract attention; ground crew / pilot communication is adjusted at a level to provide understanding. Audio signals which may be heard over the I/C are listed with the relevant system; VIWAS signals in section 3.

Recorders

HUD camera: control signals from the fire control system trigger camera operation (GAF T.O. 1F-MIG29-34-1).

Flight data recorder (FDR / TESTER): records flight parameters and the operation of important aircraft systems. Conservation of recorded data is assured under: impact with g-forces up to 1 000 · temperatures up to 1 000 °C for 15 minutes · exposure to sea water up to 5 days · exposure to fuel up to two days.

Powered by 28.5 VDC; recording is made of the last three hours of aircraft operation. Activated manually with the RECORD switch on the RH console; if not activated manually, automatic operation starts at or above 85 % engine RPM with the trailing edge flaps down, or if the weight is off the right main gear at any RPM.

Data are transferred to the ground evaluation system without extracting the tape, at a rate 8–12 times faster than the recording, for an express analysis containing: aircraft number · flight number · date of flight · sequence number of the malfunction · channel number for recorded data and extreme values · start and end time of occurrences or malfunctions. Additionally available: graphical display of coded values and a print-out of all malfunctions.
